readerTitle: Your new customer paid you $120. You're still in the hole.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (빵 정기배송 베이커리, 프로젝트 관리 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 새 고객은 매출이 쌓일 때가 아니라 남는 돈이 획득 비용을 갚을 때 비로소 본전이 되며, 그 기간이 길수록 성장은 현금을 더 깊이 판다.
misconception: 고객이 낸 돈이 획득 비용을 넘으면 본전을 찾은 것이다. 획득 비용이 싼 채널이 늘 더 좋은 채널이다.

sources.text: 관리회계·단위경제의 표준 개념 (고객 획득 비용 회수 기간, CAC payback)

factChecks.note: 베이커리: 월 남는 돈 $40 − $25 = $15, 회수 기간 $90 ÷ $15 = 6개월. 매출 기준으로 잘못 계산하면 $90 ÷ $40 = 2.25개월. 3개월 시점 매출 누계 $120, 남는 돈 누계 $45, 아직 $45 부족.

월 100명 획득 시 현금 구멍: 각 코호트는 획득 월에 $9,000을 쓰고 다음 달부터 월 $1,500을 돌려준다고 가정. 누적 현금 1개월 −9,000, 2개월 −16,500, 3개월 −22,500, 4개월 −27,000, 5개월 −30,000, 6개월 −31,500, 7개월 −31,500, 8개월 −30,000. 카드에는 "over $30,000", "about six months"로 적었습니다.
소프트웨어: 광고 채널 $300 ÷ ($50 − $10 = $40) = 7.5개월. 파트너 채널 $600 ÷ ($150 − $30 = $120) = 5개월. 두 채널 고객이 평균 약 2년 유지된다는 가정.

cards.title: Your new customer paid you $120. You're still in the hole.
body: A bakery spends $90 on flyers and a free first box to win one bread-box subscriber. The subscriber pays $40 a month.
Three months in, they've paid $120. The owner feels the $90 is long recovered. It isn't. Not even close.

image.label: A bread box on a doorstep next to a small hole in the ground
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 현관 앞 빵 상자 옆에 작은 구덩이가 있고, 동전이 하나씩 구덩이를 채우는 중. 구덩이는 아직 절반만 찼음. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: When does this subscriber pay back the $90?
body: Each $40 box costs the bakery $25 in flour, butter, packaging and delivery.
How long until this customer has paid back the $90 it cost to win them?

options.feedback: That counts every dollar the customer pays. But $25 of each $40 goes straight back out to make and deliver the box.
Right. Only $15 a month is left after the box's own costs. $90 ÷ $15 = 6 months.

options.text: It depends on how long they stay
options.feedback: True that if they leave early, the $90 never comes back. But the time to pay back is fixed by the numbers: about 6 months.

cards.title: Follow one subscriber.
body: After three months the customer has paid $120, but only **$45** of it is left over. The bakery is still $45 short.

breakdown.label: Cost to win
breakdown.detail: Flyers and the free first box

cards.title: Payback period
body: The **payback period** is how long it takes for what a customer leaves you each month to add up to what it cost to win them.
The math is one line: cost to win a customer ÷ what they leave each month after the costs of serving them.
Use what's left, not the price. Revenue makes payback look three times faster than it is here.

image.label: A rising line crossing zero at month six
image.brief: 누적 현금 그래프. 0개월에 −$90에서 시작해 매달 $15씩 올라가 6개월에 0선을 넘는 계단형 선. 0선을 넘는 지점에 "Paid back" 라벨. 옆에 흐린 점선으로 매출 기준 선(2개월대에 0선 통과)을 "Looks like"로 표시.

cards.title: Growth digs the hole deeper first.
body: Until payback, every new customer is cash you've spent and not yet earned back.

Say the bakery wins 100 subscribers a month. It spends $9,000 every month, while earlier groups return just $1,500 each. The hole keeps deepening for about six months, to **over $30,000**, before it starts to close.
The longer the payback, the more cash you need to grow. Many profitable-on-paper businesses run out of money this way.

image.label: Stacked holes getting deeper month by month
image.brief: 월별로 나란히 놓인 구덩이 6개가 점점 깊어지다가 7번째부터 얕아지는 일러스트. 가장 깊은 구덩이에 "−$31,500" 라벨.

cards.title: How to shorten the wait.
body: Payback has only two inputs, plus one timing trick:
list: **Spend less to win each customer:** referrals, partners, better-targeted ads
**Keep more each month:** raise the price or cut the cost of serving
**Get paid upfront:** a customer who prepays three months gives you $45 of margin on day one
cards.callout: Each lever shrinks the cash hole, not just the number.
cards.softwareNote: Software companies often push annual plans paid upfront for this reason. A year of cash on day one can mean payback before the customer has even logged in much.

cards.title: Payback tells you how fast, not how much.
body: A 6-month payback means nothing if most subscribers cancel at month 4. Check how long customers actually stay before trusting the number.
It also ignores everything after payback. A customer who pays back in 3 months and leaves in 4 earns you little. One who takes 8 months and stays five years may be worth far more.
Use payback to judge cash and risk. Use lifetime value to judge worth.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your project-management app has two ways to win customers. Both groups stay about two years. You have nine months of cash.

**Ads:** $300 per customer, who pays $50 a month and costs $10 to serve. **Partners:** $600 per customer, a bigger team paying $150 a month and costing $30 to serve. Where do you put next quarter's budget?

options.text: Ads. They cost half as much per customer
options.feedback: Cheaper to win, but each customer leaves only $40 a month, so payback takes 7.5 months. That's close to your nine months of cash.
$600 ÷ $120 = 5 months, so cash comes back faster even though each customer costs more. The risk is depending on a few partners.

options.text: Split the budget evenly to stay safe
options.feedback: Spreading bets has value, but half your money goes to the channel that ties up cash longest when cash is your tightest limit.

cards.title: A customer pays back when what's left covers what you spent.
body: Divide the cost to win a customer by what they leave each month. That's how long your cash is out, and how much growing faster will cost you.
**Try it today:** take your main way of winning customers. Divide what it costs per customer by what one customer leaves you each month. Is the answer shorter than how long they stay?
